final_proof:
Let $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}$ be a continuous complex function. We can write $f(t)$ in terms of its real and imaginary parts as $f(t) = u(t) + i v(t)$, where $u, v: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ are real-valued functions.

Since $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, its real part $u$ and imaginary part $v$ are also continuous real-valued functions on $[a, b]$.

By the definition of the definite integral of a complex-valued function of a real variable, the integral of $f$ over an interval is the sum of the integral of its real part and $i$ times the integral of its imaginary part:
$$ \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f(t) \,dt = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} u(t) \,dt + i \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} v(t) \,dt $$
for any interval $[\alpha, \beta] \subseteq [a, b]$.

Applying this definition to the intervals $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$, we have:
$$ \int_a^c f(t) \,dt + \int_c^b f(t) \,dt = \left( \int_a^c u(t) \,dt + i \int_a^c v(t) \,dt \right) + \left( \int_c^b u(t) \,dt + i \int_c^b v(t) \,dt \right) $$

By the commutativity and associativity of complex addition, we can rearrange the terms on the right-hand side to group the integrals of the real and imaginary parts:
$$ = \left( \int_a^c u(t) \,dt + \int_c^b u(t) \,dt \right) + i \left( \int_a^c v(t) \,dt + \int_c^b v(t) \,dt \right) $$

Since $u$ and $v$ are continuous real-valued functions on $[a, b]$, and $c \in [a, b]$, we can use the property of additivity of the definite integral on adjacent intervals for real functions. This property states that for any integrable function $g$ on $[a, b]$ and $c \in [a, b]$, $\int_a^c g(t) \,dt + \int_c^b g(t) \,dt = \int_a^b g(t) \,dt$.

Applying this property to $u$ and $v$ yields:
$$ = \int_a^b u(t) \,dt + i \int_a^b v(t) \,dt $$

Finally, applying the definition of the complex integral in reverse, this expression is exactly the integral of $f$ over $[a, b]$:
$$ = \int_a^b f(t) \,dt $$

Therefore, $\int_a^c f(t) \,dt + \int_c^b f(t) \,dt = \int_a^b f(t) \,dt$, which completes the proof.
